'''''Senecio hispidulus''''', the '''hill fireweed''' or '''rough groundsel''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Asteraceae|daisy]] family. It is found in many parts of [[Australia]].<ref name=robinson>Les Robinson - Field Guide to the Native Plants of Sydney, {{ISBN|978-0-7318-1211-0}} page142</ref><ref name=Plantnet>{{cite web|last=Harden|first=Gwen|title=''Senecio hispidulus''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Senecio~hispidulus|work=Plant Net - NSW Flora Online|publisher=NSW Government|access-date=November 12, 2012}}</ref>

==Description==
''Senecio hispidulus'' is an erect [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] with an [[Annual plant|annual]] or a short lived [[Perennial plant|perennial]] life cycle and can grow up to {{Convert|2|m}} tall, but is usually between {{Convert|30-100|cm|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="nzpcn.org.nz">New Zealand Plant Conservation Network (2018). ''Senecio hispidulus''. Retrieved 06/04/2018 from http://nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=2257.</ref> It is a [[dicotyledon]]ous herb which means the plant is [[Vascular plant|vascular]] and that it [[flower]]s. The plant flowers many small [[inflorescence]] of a yellow or pale-yellow color. The herb is sparsely to moderately course-hairy, with shorter hairs on upper leaf surface and longer, denser and jointed hairs on lower surface (A. Rich, 1834){{citation needed|date=December 2018}}. The primary [[Plant stem|stem]] is usually simple and is covered in conspicuous soft bristly hairs. ''S. hispidulus'' has a woody base which develops into a ribbed mid stem.  Mid stem leaves are evenly spaced and sized, usually {{Convert|70-150|mm|abbr=on}} in length. Its leaf color varying from dark green to yellow green and sometimes shaded with red. Also upper stem can be tinged with purple or red, and is usually triggered by environmental temperatures. The larger and lower leaf margins are [[Leaf#Sinuate|sinuately]] [[Pinnation|pinnately]] [[Glossary of leaf morphology#lobed|lobed]] being usually three to five [[Glossary of botanical terms#toothed|toothed]], having a terminal tooth which is longer than that of the laterals. The uppermost smaller leaves, more in proximity to plant inflorescence are often [[Leaf#Dentate|dentate]] and not lobed. Plant inflorescence usually of many [[Pseudanthium#Related terms|capitula]] (flower heads).<ref name="auto">Webb, C. J., Skyes, W. R., Garnock-Jones P. J. (1988). Naturalized Pteridophytes,</ref> Overall number of capitula contained usually between 14 and 48 containing 25 [[Glossary of botanical terms#floret|florets]] per capitula.<ref name="auto2">Drury, D. G. (1974). Illustrated and Annotated Key of Erechtitoid Senecios in New Zealand (Senecioneae-Compositae) With a Description of ''Senecio diaschides''. New Zealand journal of botany, 12:4, 513-540.</ref> Although this can be dependent on which component of ''S. hispidulus'' is found in [[New Zealand]]. Mature floret size usually between 6 mm and 12 mm long and 4 mm wide. The more mature and lobed leaves carry a very distinctive look to them, being a relatively narrow leaf. It has between 2 and 5 lobes along the side margins of the leaf.  The seeds of ''S. hispidulus'' are hairy, which can be related to its name in [[Latin]] where {{lang|la|senecio}} means 'old man' which can be linked to the 'bearded' or hairy seeds. ''S. hispidulus'' has small seeds usually around 0.5 mm wide and 2 mm long.  In New Zealand ''S. hispidulus'' is represented by two components.<ref name="auto2"/> These two components are geographically segregated as one grows in the area north of 39° south, where the other component grows to the south from that point. The main differences between the two components include the number of capitula and the number of florets per capitula counted on a mature plant. The northern component having 14 capitula counted, which contain between 26 and 31 florets each. Whereas the southern component counts 48 capitula with between 17 and 24 florets on each capitula.<ref name="auto2"/>

==Distribution==
===Natural global range===
''S. hispidulus'' is [[Indigenous (ecology)|indigenous]] to New Zealand and Australia. In Australia it is predominantly found in the state of [[New South Wales]]. Although ''S. hispidulus'' is also found in [[Tasmania]], [[Western Australia]], and [[Queensland]].

===New Zealand range===
In the [[North Island]] the dominant ranges of ''S. hispidulus'' are vicinity of [[Auckland isthmus]], [[Coromandel Peninsula|Coromandel]], [[Ōpōtiki]], and [[Wellington Province]] (A. Rich, 1934){{citation needed|date=December 2018}}. In the [[South Island]] plant range includes [[Nelson, New Zealand|Nelson]], [[Marlborough Region|Marlborough]], and [[Canterbury, New Zealand|North Canterbury]]. Although there is some variation in two recognized components among New Zealand material of ''S. hispidulus'' which has been collected. Whereby [[D. G. Drury]] suggests that the plants in the north of the North Island may have been naturalized in New Zealand, whereas there is little evidence to decide whether the plants from the northern South Island and Wellington area are indigenous or [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]].<ref name="auto"/> As stated before the two components of ''S. hispidulus'' are geographically dispersed as there is a documented break in the range of ''S. hispidulus'' between latitude 38° and 40° south which separates the two components of ''S. hispidulus''. This fact therefore does not support the [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]] hypothesis, which according to Drury "lacks support" on geographical basis.<ref name="auto2"/>

===Habitat preference===
The habitat of ''S. hispidulus'' can vary from [[coast]]al to [[Montane ecosystems|montane]] environments, especially in sites where indigenous vegetation are [[Fire ecology|burned]] or [[Deforestation|cleared]] recently.<ref name="auto1">Lan Popay, Paul Champion, Trevor James (2010).Common Weeds of New Zealand. New Zealand Plant Protection Society</ref> Usually growing in altitudes from [[sea level]] to {{Convert|457|m|sigfig=3}} above sea level.<ref name="auto2"/> The herb is prevalent in dry bare or disturbed habitats, such as recently cleared or burned areas. Primarily found in unstable environment. Also [[Woodland edge|forest margins]], coastal sites, and [[Stream bed|riverbeds]] are common place for ''S. hispidulus''.<ref>Webb, C. J., Skyes, W. R., Garnock-Jones P. J. (1988). Naturalized Pteridophytes</ref>

==Life cycle and phenology==
''S. hispidulus'' can grow all year round depending on environmental circumstances, which is one of the reasons various specimens can have different heights. Some plants in good growing conditions can grow all year round, whereas other plants in suboptimal conditions will not be able to do this. This fact is one example of the versatility of the herb, which is able to easily adapt to its environment. This versatility is also demonstrated in the flowering period of ''S. hispidulus'' which is estimated to be from October to April, but is differently assessed by [[New Zealand Plant Conservation Network]] to last from August to May which is a very large time period for flowering to occur.<ref>Flora of New Zealand, Volume IV, 281-282. Botany Division DSIR, Christchurch.</ref><ref name="nzpcn.org.nz"/> But it is safe to say the plant flowers usually between spring and summer. ''S. hispidulus'' is known to be a strongly [[invasive species]] which is easily grown from seed. When flowering ''S. hispidulus'' produces both [[wikt:polliniferous|polliniferous]] (pollen bearing) florets and female florets. This is likely to increase the plants' probability to reproduce in a scenario where cross pollination might be hindered. A distinction in the number of polliniferous florets to female florets has been discovered between the two different components of ''S. hispidulus'' in New Zealand.<ref name="auto2"/> The Northern component of ''S. hispidulus'' has been documented to grow between nine and eleven polliniferous florets per capitulum (cluster of small florets), whereas the southern component is recorded to carry between five and eight polliniferous florets per capitulum. Both the northern and southern components carry a more equal number of female florets compared to the florets with the polliniferous stamen. This might indicate a different need for pollen carrying flowers between the two ''S. hispidulus'' components in New Zealand.

==Diet/prey/predators==
===Diet and foraging===
''S. hispidulus'' like to grow in forest margins and clearings, disturbed [[pasture]], coastal sites, and waste places.<ref name="auto1"/> It grows in [[Arable land|arable]] and waste land, gardens.<ref name=Parham>B.E.V.Parham, A.J.Healy(1976).common weeds in New Zealand .A.R.shearer, government printer, wellington, New Zealand</ref>  Easily grown in fresh seed. The plant grows on many types of soil and can survival in large ranges of habitats.<ref name=LeRoy/> The optimum temperature of germination is at {{Convert|25|C}} while the greatest flush of germination is at {{Convert|9|C}}.<ref name="LeRoy">LeRoy Holm, Jerry Doll, Eric Holm, Juan Pancho, James Herberger (1997). world weeds. Library of congress</ref> The maximum temperature of germination is about 35 °C.<ref name=LeRoy/> It is reported by Koch(1970),{{citation needed|date=December 2018}} better germination with alternating low and high temperature. Only if giving some light to seeds, it can germinate, and even intermittent low level of daylight is sufficient.<ref name=LeRoy/> Fireweed is very weedy and invasive.

===Predators, parasites, and diseases===
''S. hispidulus'' often has a [[Rust (fungus)|rust fungus]] attacking it. [[Host (biology)|Hosts]] of magpie moth, ''[[Nyctemera annulata]]''.<ref name=Parham/> It is very weedy and invasive. Potentially [[poison]]ous, but not usually eaten by [[Livestock|stock]].<ref name="auto1"/> [[Cattle]], [[horse]]s, and several other livestock animals may eat it.<ref name=LeRoy/>

==Other information==
===Control===
''S. hispidulus'' is normally easy to control. In most situations, the ways people use to control weeds are divided into two groups. The one is chemical ways like using [[herbicide]]s, the other is physical ways like [[shading]]. But fireweed is resistant to some kinds of herbicides which is usually used in cropping, such as [[trifluralin]], [[oryzalin]], [[pendimethalin]], and [[bromacil]].<ref name="massey">{{cite web | url=http://www.massey.ac.nz/massey/learning/colleges/college-of-sciences/clinics-and-services/weeds-database/weeds-database_home.cfm | title=Weeds Database - Massey University}}</ref> As a plant which only has a shallow and fibrous [[root system]], hill fireweed is easily controlled by pulling out from land or using a [[Hoe (tool)|hoe]].<ref name="massey" /> However the seeds of fireweed can be delivered too quickly by wind to control, which means if a fireweed or a seed of it escape from land cleaning, it will take up the land again and people will fail to control it.<ref name="massey" /> What is more, [[lawn mower]] is also used instead of handing. Shading is an easy and efficient way to control it. Using [[mulch]] to cover the land where fireweed is found will prevent seed from germinating from in soil.<ref name="massey" /> And people should be careful about preventing seeds from blowing on the top of the mulch and kill first few plants which grow on the top of mulch as soon as possible.<ref name="massey" /> All in all, weeds need to be stopped setting seed around the container plants, or else seeds will germinate in the sterile [[Potting soil|potting mix]] planter bags, and it will cause problems.<ref name="massey" />

===Poisoning===
It is believed to lead to more livestock poisoning and death (Heywood 1978, Lawrence 1981).{{citation needed|date=December 2018}}
''Senecio'' species of plants are containing [[pyrrolizidine alkaloid]]s (PA) which is harmful for human.<ref name=LeRoy/> Because they lead to the damages of liver and lungs, they are related to poisonings and losses.<ref name=LeRoy/> PA may be considered as one kind of [[carcinogenesis]].<ref name=LeRoy/>

===Herbicides resistance===
''S. hispidulus'' have surprising adaptability which make it remain with human, it means fireweeds often survival from controlling and weeds again. From 1900s, people noticed the pesticides resistance by diseases and insects.<ref name=LeRoy/> And 50 years later, the resistance of pesticide became widespread with the use of synthetic organic [[pesticide]]s.<ref name=LeRoy/> It means even though higher concentration of pesticides had been used to control fireweeds, it became inefficient. It was shown in 1973 that [[simazine]] and related compounds stop [[photosynthesis]] in susceptible (S) [[biotype]] but not efficient in resistant (R) biotype.<ref name=LeRoy/> In S-plant the herbicide set relationships between [[protein]] and [[Electron transport chain|electron transport]] in [[photosystem]] is inhibited.<ref name=LeRoy/> By around 1985, some reports showing that there were relationships between [[triazine]]-resistance and decrease productivity in some way.<ref name=LeRoy/> Whatever under non-competitive or competitive situations, R-plants have more leaf area tissue and a better leaf area ratio, but R-plant have less productive tissue than S-plant.<ref name=LeRoy/> All in all, S-biotype fireweed is greater productors not only of biomass but also of reproductive structures.<ref name=LeRoy/> In 1987, it found that in more than 2 cm depth of soil, R-fireweed have greater longevity than S-fireweed while in 0 to 2 cm depth of soil, both biotypes demonstrated different longevity according to the environment and management practices.<ref name=LeRoy/>
